Minha leitura é outra camada do problema.

Quando a IA consegue gerar a planta, o desafio deixa de ser “ela desenha?” e vira “isso entra no processo real da empresa?”. Porque em engenharia, saída bonita não basta. Precisa conversar com regra técnica, software de entrega, revisão e fluxo operacional.

É exatamente aí que muita iniciativa trava. A demo funciona. A operação não.

Foi esse tipo de problema que eu já resolvi na Consult Eng, empresa brasileira de engenharia sanitária: automação de Revit que gera modelos de estações elevatórias de esgoto, com Revit rodando sem tela, na nuvem, via APS Design Automation.

No fim, o valor não está em impressionar no prompt. Está em colocar a automação dentro do processo que já precisa acontecer.

en.title: Generating a floor plan in minutes doesn’t solve the whole project
en.caption:
TechCrunch featured a startup that says it can generate blueprints ready for approval in minutes from a 2D sketch or PDF. The proposal is clear: take time away from drafting and give that time back to design. According to the source, architects spend 80% of their time on drafting.

My take is a different layer of the problem.

When AI can generate the plan, the challenge stops being “can it draw?” and becomes “does this fit into the company’s real process?”. Because in engineering, nice-looking output is not enough. It has to work with technical rules, delivery software, review, and the operational workflow.

That is exactly where many initiatives get stuck. The demo works. The operation doesn’t.

That is the kind of problem I have already solved at Consult Eng, a Brazilian sanitary engineering company: Revit automation that generates models of sewage pumping stations, with Revit running headless in the cloud via APS Design Automation.

In the end, the value is not in impressing with a prompt. It is in putting automation inside the process that already needs to happen.
